A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MetSelect research. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and references support reliable comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains a separate appendix.

before.justification: V1 reports original node-classification experiments on ten datasets, including comparisons across three GNN architectures, depth and poisoning tests, ablations, and runtime measurements.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds self-loop results and comparisons with JKNet aggregation methods.

M1.justification: Section 7.5 adds an adaptation that selects among LSTM-, concatenation-, and max-pooled representations instead of ordinary GNN layers. The core prototype-distance selector remains unchanged. Equation 7 explicitly documents a distance loss already mentioned, but undefined, in v1's depth experiment; its disclosure alone does not establish a new training procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate transductive node classification on the same ten datasets and retain the depth and poisoning scenarios. The added self-loop and aggregation experiments change model or preprocessing settings within that coverage, without adding datasets, populations, or tasks.

E2.justification: V2 Table 5 newly compares JKNet-Max, JKNet-Cat, and JKNet-LSTM against JKNet-MetSelect. These aggregation comparators differ from the modified hard-selection AttnSelect already evaluated in v1. The original Table 2 comparator set is unchanged.

E3.justification: V2 adds evaluations with a self-loop on every node and with pooled JKNet representations as selection candidates. Existing splits, training budgets, and metrics remain unchanged. Section 7.3 also changes the reported robustness-training loss from cross-entropy Equation 6 to distance-loss Equation 7; the unchanged Figure 4 does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Section 7.4 and Table 4 add a self-loop analysis testing whether gains persist when each aggregation includes the node's own features. Section 7.2 additionally reports similar behavior with the linear-decoder loss through depth eight. Existing layer-selection ablations, depth tests, poisoning tests, runtime analysis, and layer-distribution analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Both retain ten random splits except for ogbn-arxiv and identical standard-deviation reporting in Table 2. New Table 4 follows that convention, while Table 5 supplies point estimates only. No new run counts, seeds, uncertainty-estimation procedures, or significance tests are specified.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 and Figures 3–5 retain their results. New Table 4 reports mixed self-loop outcomes: MetSelect versus FinalSelect is 76.67 versus 61.96 on Wisconsin, but 83.72 versus 86.18 on Cora. Table 5 reports a smaller average gap from the best score for JKNet-MetSelect, 0.009 versus JKNet-Cat's 0.011 on the F1/100 scale. These are additional results under new settings.

T1.justification: V1 only notes online updates in its space-complexity discussion. V2 explicitly gives storage bounds of O(L|Y|d) for means and O(Ld²) for covariance matrices, arguing that this overhead is independent of node count. It also supplies the previously missing formal distance-loss definition. Existing problem definitions, Equations 1–6, and time-complexity analysis remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contribution and claims: personalized layer selection improves GNN classification, supports greater depth, and increases poisoning robustness in a plug-and-play manner. The additional experiments do not redefine that core framing.

C2.justification: V2 explains limited homophilic gains through unchanged representation power, motivates the pooled-representation comparison with aggregation methods, and acknowledges the difficulty of proving layer optimality. It also interprets self-loop gains as consistently higher, although Table 4 shows higher MetSelect means on only four of ten datasets.

D1.justification: V2 specifies the distance-loss formula, its margin α = 1, and cross-entropy as the default loss; v1 referred to the distance loss through an unresolved equation citation. Hardware, optimizer, epochs, and learning-rate choices are retained. V2 removes the IP-approval footnote but retains the promise of code after publication; neither PDF supplies a code-release link.

R1.justification: V2 adds Rossi et al. (2024), 'Edge directionality improves learning on heterophilic graphs.' It also expands positioning against layer aggregation by discussing representation-space and dimension requirements and presenting MetSelect as complementary to aggregation. The broader related-work structure remains unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized language and cross-reference edits, renames Problem 2, adds subsection 7.5 and explanatory paragraphs, shortens one author's displayed name, and adds publication information. Most existing prose and the overall section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 4–5 and repositions existing tables and figures as text flows across pages. All five figures retain their graphical content; Figure 1's caption now identifies gray users as unlabeled. Publication headers and front matter also change, without a broad visual redesign.

improvement.justification: V2 improves technical completeness by supplying the missing distance-loss definition and explicit storage bounds, and adds useful self-loop and aggregation comparisons. The gain is limited by inconsistent loss references in Section 7.2 and an overstated self-loop interpretation: Table 4 favors MetSelect on only four of ten datasets. These issues temper, but do not outweigh, the added documentation and evidence.
